scope: thr_6_B_driven: mechanisms where field amplitude B or B-direction (or B relative to a static B0), rather than dB/dt or induced E, is the putative driver: radical pair / cryptochrome / flavin; ion cyclotron and ion parametric resonance incl. combined fields and Prato snail/mouse work; biogenic magnetite; static-field (SMF) diamagnetic/gradient effects and SMF pain trials; Lorentz/Hall/MHD; B-dependent dose-response, static-bias effects and credibility of microtesla ELF effects; plus a decision-test record contrasting B-driven and E-driven designs.

targets.name: Radical-pair (flavin/superoxide) ROS partitioning by weak static field plus RF/Zeeman-resonant field
targets.driver_explanation: In the NIST/Nevada/Montana line of work the response needs a static field of about 45 uT AND an oscillating field of about 10 uT rms at 5-10 MHz oriented perpendicular to it; the response depends on orientation and on the RF being near the Zeeman/hyperfine condition, i.e. on the ratio and geometry of B_AC to B0, not on RF induction. For scale, the RF dB/dt is very large (computed 6e2-9e2 T/s peak) yet the cell-scale induced E is only mV/m (computed, r=10 um assumed), so induction is not a plausible driver in these designs, and therapeutic PEMF (kHz-range, mT) does not match the RF/Zeeman conditions. Theory papers (Kattnig 2016; Brocklehurst 1996) argue spin relaxation and radical lifetime limit such effects, and the extension to broadband pulsed fields is speculative.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Static 45 uT plus 7 MHz RF at 10 uT rms vs static-only control (rat PASMC)
discriminating_evidence.finding: Superoxide fell and H2O2 rose only with the combined static+RF exposure; sham used only for DC (abstract + partial full text).

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Static 45 uT vertical, RF 5 or 10 MHz at 10 uT rms perpendicular to static, vs static-only controls (HT1080)
discriminating_evidence.finding: 10 MHz plus static cut cell number up to 30% (day 2) and raised H2O2 55% at 8 h versus static-only controls; 5 MHz also tested.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: RF at Zeeman resonance, varied field orientation (HUVEC)
discriminating_evidence.finding: ROS partitioning and bioenergetics changed with oscillating-field orientation, as expected for coherent singlet-triplet mixing and not for induced currents.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: 7 MHz field applied at 0, 24 and 48 degrees to the geomagnetic field (robins)
discriminating_evidence.finding: Orientation was normal when the RF was parallel to the geomagnetic field and lost at 24 and 48 degrees, so the effect depends on angle between B_AC and B0 (resonance-like), not on RF amplitude alone.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Spin-relaxation simulation, Arabidopsis cryptochrome-1
discriminating_evidence.finding: Radical-pair lifetimes near microseconds are optimal and relaxation is too fast for the long coherence needed to explain RF disruption; counter-evidence from theory.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Radical-pair theory of environmental-strength fields
discriminating_evidence.finding: Low-field effects depend on radical lifetime and chemistry; freely diffusing radical pairs unlikely to give significant biological effects.

targets.name: Radical-pair magnetic field effect at mT amplitudes (flavin photochemistry, cryptochrome)
targets.driver_explanation: In vitro flavin/cell photochemistry shows a magnetic-field effect whose size depends on the instantaneous field amplitude B and saturates at a few mT to tens of mT (B1/2 = 18.0 mT in HeLa autofluorescence; effects at 100 mT in Drosophila neurons); the effect is a property of static or slowly varying B, not of dB/dt. Because radical-pair lifetimes are microseconds (Kattnig 2016) while PEMF pulse widths are hundreds of microseconds to ms, a PEMF peak field in the 1-50 mT range would act on a light-activated radical pair as a quasi-static field during each pulse (my inference, not tested for pulses in these papers). All these systems need photoexcitation, so relevance to non-illuminated deep tissue is uncertain.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Field sweep up to 25 mT, single-cell fluorescence kinetics (HeLa)
discriminating_evidence.finding: Autofluorescence changed with static field, half-saturation 18.0 mT, saturation 3.7%; consistent with triplet-born radical pair.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: FAD photochemistry vs pH 2.3-8.0 in water
discriminating_evidence.finding: Magnetic field effects persist at physiological pH at about 25% of the pH 2.3 sensitivity.

discriminating_evidence.finding: Depolarisation, input-resistance rise and firing were potentiated by the field only in combination with blue-light cryptochrome activation; single field strength tested.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Model carotenoid-porphyrin-fullerene triad, 50 uT or less
discriminating_evidence.finding: Radical-pair lifetime changed at geomagnetic-strength fields with anisotropy; proof of principle, not a biological readout.

targets.name: Cryptochrome-dependent responses to ELF/pulsed fields (ROS, circadian, behaviour, plant growth)
targets.driver_explanation: The best discriminating design is Fedele 2014: in a shielded apparatus a 300 uT static field, 3 Hz and 50 Hz fields all produced the same circadian-period shortening in Drosophila, and 3 Hz was effective from 90 to 1000 uT; a static field has dB/dt = 0 (and 50 Hz at 300 uT would have about 17-fold larger dB/dt than 3 Hz, computed), so B amplitude, not dB/dt or induced E, is the operative variable there. Plant data (500 uT static) are likewise B-driven. Sherrard 2018 used a 10 Hz pulsed device of about 2 mT peak, cryptochrome knock-out and a mu-metal control; those controls prove field-dependence and cryptochrome-dependence but do not discriminate B from dB/dt, because shielding or an antiparallel coil removes both B and the induced E together. Lohof 2022 reports that low-intensity rTMS repair depends on the stimulation pattern and on cryptochrome (abstract only).

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Static 300 uT vs 3 Hz vs 50 Hz in a shielded Schuderer apparatus with sham; 90, 300, 1000 uT at 3 Hz; CRY mutants; blue vs 500 nm light
discriminating_evidence.finding: Static, 3 Hz and 50 Hz gave the same period effect (dB/dt differs from 0 to computed 0.094 T/s), so B, not dB/dt; effect is CRY- and blue-light-dependent; hyperactivity not significant at 1 mT; 500 nm light reversed the sign; mouse SCN slices showed no effect at 50-500 uT, 50 Hz.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Cry1/2 knock-out/knock-down, DmCry expression, mu-metal (1 mm, field reduced about 85%), antiparallel-wound coil with same current
discriminating_evidence.finding: ROS rose within 15 min in Cry-expressing cells and cells lacking Cry did not respond; mu-metal and antiparallel coil abolished it. Shielding and antiparallel coil remove B and induced E together, so B vs dB/dt/E is not resolved.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: LI-rTMS pattern comparison in cerebellum, Cry dependence
discriminating_evidence.finding: Repair depended on stimulation pattern and Cry, not on induced-current excitation (abstract only).

discriminating_evidence.finding: 500 uT enhanced blue-light, cryptochrome-dependent hypocotyl inhibition; no effect in the dark, under red light or in cry mutants.

targets.name: Ion cyclotron / ion parametric resonance (Ca2+ and other ions) in combined static + AC fields
targets.driver_explanation: The ICR/IPR hypothesis says the response depends on the AC frequency relative to f_c = qB0/(2*pi*m) and on the ratio B_AC/B0 (Lednev 1991; Blanchard & Blackman 1994), not on dB/dt or induced E. Supporting designs vary B0, f and B_AC independently and test orientation: PC-12 neurite outgrowth followed IPR predictions at 45 Hz/36.6 uT and 25 Hz/20.3 uT with an off-resonance control (Blackman 1994); chick brain Ca2+ efflux required B_dc perpendicular to B_ac at constant E (Blackman 1990); rat behaviour followed proportional DC and AC scaling at 50 and 500 uT (Zhadin 1999). Against it, several well-designed attempts found nothing (Parkinson 1989; Coulton 1993), one diatom study was irreproducible (Reese 1991), and physics critiques show classical cyclotron orbits cannot survive collisions (Sandweiss 1990: gyration radius about 50 m, damping time below 1e-10 s; Halle 1988; Adair 1992). Machlup 2007 and Engstrom 1996 try to rescue the theory.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Independent control of B_ac (7.7-46.8 uT rms), B_dc (36.6 uT or 2 uT off-resonance), f (45 vs 25 Hz) in a multi-coil system
discriminating_evidence.finding: All PC-12 neurite outgrowth responses matched IPR predictions, including the off-resonance condition.

discriminating_evidence.finding: Ca2+ efflux from chick brain only when perpendicular; orientation matters while E magnitude is the same.

discriminating_evidence.finding: Outcome was enhancement, reduction or null depending on temperature history, which may explain poor reproducibility.

discriminating_evidence.finding: Current peak (20-30%) at the cyclotron frequency, proportional to B0 and only at very low B_ac (higher amplitudes abolished it).

targets.name: Combined static + low-frequency AC magnetic field (CMF) signalling in bone cells (Ca2+ flux, IGF-II)
targets.driver_explanation: Fitzsimmons and colleagues report that a combined AC/DC field at about 15 Hz, with a calculated induced potential gradient of only 1e-5 V/m in medium, increases Ca2+ flux, IGF-II receptor number and IGF-II release in osteoblast-like cells, with a narrow frequency peak (15.3-16.3 Hz, bandwidth about 1 Hz). The 1e-5 V/m E is far below usual cellular E thresholds, so the authors argue for resonance-type dynamics, cell shape and signal averaging rather than simple induction. This is an ICR/IPR-type B_AC/B0 dependence, but B_ac and B_dc values were not in the abstracts and the work is from a single lab.

targets.name: Land-snail / mouse opioid-analgesia inhibition by ELF fields (resonance-like, light-dependent, Ca2+/NO)
targets.driver_explanation: The Prato/Kavaliers snail work reports amplitude windows (nonlinear in B_ac over 0-547 uT at 60 Hz), frequency windows at fixed 141 uT (30-35, 60-90, 120-240 Hz), dependence on the parallel static field, and angle dependence between AC (299 uT peak) and DC (78 uT) fields. The authors argue this excludes induced current (it would be constant with angle at fixed B_ac) and excludes magnetite torque (maximum would be at 90 degrees), and favour a Lednev-type parametric resonance with Ca2+ or K+ settings, a light requirement and NO involvement. A parallel line in rodents used rotating 0.5 Hz fields (0.15-0.8 mT; computed dB/dt up to 2.5e-3 T/s) and Ca2+-channel drugs.

targets.name: Mouse detection of ambient ELF magnetic field removal (mu-metal shielding analgesia) and B x f threshold
targets.driver_explanation: This is the clearest quantitative B-vs-dB/dt test in the scope. Mu-metal shielding for 1 h/day induces naloxone-reversible analgesia in mice, and reintroducing 30 or 120 Hz fields of 25-500 nT peak attenuates it. At a constant B_pk x f product of 6000 nT-Hz (12.5-100 Hz) the attenuation was constant, so the detector responds to the B x f product, i.e. dB/dt (or induced current), not to B amplitude; the threshold is at or below 1000 nT-Hz (computed dB/dt_pk about 6.3e-6 T/s). Independent replication (Choleris 2002, Pisa and London) shows that nulling only the static component (Helmholtz coils) or screening only E does not reproduce shielding, implying the very weak time-varying magnetic component matters. Blue/UV light is required, so a photoreceptor-based mechanism is proposed.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Reintroduced 30 and 120 Hz fields (25-500 nT pk) and constant 6000 nT-Hz at 12.5, 25, 50, 100 Hz in a shielded box
discriminating_evidence.finding: Attenuation scaled with amplitude at fixed frequency and was constant at fixed B x f: dependence on nT-Hz (a dB/dt-like metric); threshold at or below 1000 nT-Hz.

targets.name: Specific pulsed ELF waveform (Cnp) analgesia: snails, mice, healthy humans, RA/fibromyalgia
targets.driver_explanation: The group reports that analgesia depends on the specific waveform: in snails two other pulsed designs failed to induce analgesia while Cnp (about 100 uT peak, frequency modulated, 15 min) did, with partial opioid (delta, some mu) mediation. In humans, 30 min exposures raised experimental pain thresholds (double-blind, n=39 and 31) and reduced McGill pain ratings in 13 RA and 18 FM patients (up to 400 uT peak, below 3 kHz). The data point to waveform spectral content (not B amplitude or a single dB/dt) as the determinant, but the waveform is proprietary in the abstracts and dB/dt was not reported. The related Thomas 2007 RCT is an existing library ref.

targets.name: Environmental-level 50/60 Hz microtesla fields blocking melatonin/tamoxifen action in MCF-7 cells
targets.driver_explanation: Liburdy 1993 reported a threshold between about 2 and 12 mG (0.2-1.2 uT) for 60 Hz. Harland & Liburdy 1997 used a Faraday's-law design to separate B from induced E and associated the effect with the magnetic component, not the induced E. Ishido 2001 found 1.2 uT and 100 uT identical at 50 Hz (83-fold B and dB/dt difference, same effect), indicating saturation in B instead of scaling with dB/dt; Girgert 2005 saw maximal response at 1.2 uT (non-monotonic). Independent confirmation exists (Blackman 2001, EPA; Ishido, Girgert), but 1.2 uT is below the 2 uT level that Valberg 1997 regards as implausible for a physical effect, and the original lab's earlier 1992 FEBS paper has a published erratum.

targets.name: Chick embryo teratogenic effects of microtesla pulsed fields (rise time / pulse shape)
targets.driver_explanation: Ubeda 1983 exposed chick embryos to 100 Hz pulses at 0.4-104 uT: abnormalities appeared only at 1.0 and 13.9 uT with 100 us rise time (window), and shorter rise times (2 and 42 us) at 0.4 and 1.0 uT gave bigger effects, strongest at 1.0 uT/42 us. Computed dB/dt for 1.0 uT is 0.01 T/s (100 us), 0.024 T/s (42 us) and 0.5 T/s (2 us); the non-monotonic result (42 us > 2 us) shows pulse shape/spectral content matters beyond peak dB/dt. A six-laboratory replication (Berman 1990, 1 uT, 2 us edges, 100 pps) found a small pooled excess (about 25% vs 19%) but only 2 of 6 labs were individually significant.

targets.name: Weak/static and hypomagnetic field effects via ROS and redox (planarian regeneration, metabolic mice, flavoenzymes)
targets.driver_explanation: Static fields have dB/dt = 0 by definition, so any effect is B-driven (or driven by a coincident static E). Van Huizen 2019 saw planarian regeneration go up or down with static field strength below 1 mT through ROS and Hsp70; Carter 2020 reported that a combined static magnetic (about 3 mT) plus static electric (about 7 kV/m) exposure improved glucose tolerance in mice, with 3.0 mT effective and 0.5 mT ineffective in hepatoma cells and mitochondrial SOD2 abolishing the effect; Austvold 2024 found ROS partitioning in a flavoenzyme differs between 20 nT and 50 uT. Binhi & Prato 2017 conclude that hypomagnetic effects show no consistent correlation with field magnitude, duration or type, arguing against a single common target.

discriminating_evidence.finding: Regeneration increased or decreased depending on field strength; mediated by ROS and Hsp70.

targets.name: Biogenic magnetite / magnetosome and ferritin magnetomechanical transduction
targets.driver_explanation: For magnetite-based transducers the interaction energy is mB (torque on a permanent moment) and scales with B amplitude; it does not depend on dB/dt except through viscous-lag filtering. A single-domain 50 nm magnetite cube (assumed M_s = 4.8e5 A/m, my assumption) has m = 6e-17 A m2, giving mB about 14 kT at 1 mT and 0.7 kT at 50 uT (computed at 310 K), so mT-level pulses could in principle align such particles whereas geomagnetic-strength fields cannot beat thermal noise unless chains or clusters are involved. Meister 2016 shows ferritin/MagR actuation claims are physically impossible (5-10 log units) and that only permanent-moment particles of about 30 nm and larger (magnetosomes) are plausible. Magnetite exists in human brain (kirschvink1992 in library; Gilder 2018 maps it to cerebellum and brain stem), and a strong pulse shifts bird headings via upper-beak magnetite (Wiltschko 2009).

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Physical analysis of ferritin/MagR claims (full text read)
discriminating_evidence.finding: Reported effects are 5-10 log units too large; ferritin torque 4 log units below kT at about 50 mT; permanent-moment (magnetosome-like) particles could work.

targets.name: Static magnetic field (SMF): membrane diamagnetic anisotropy, gradient forces, and SMF pain trials
targets.driver_explanation: SMF effects have dB/dt = 0 except by motion, so they are B (or B x gradient) driven. Rosen 2003 argues moderate SMF (mT to hundreds of mT) reorient diamagnetically anisotropic membrane phospholipids and deform Ca2+ and Na+ channels; Zablotskii 2016 theory suggests about 1 T with gradient up to 1 GT/m could shift membrane potential (far from permanent-magnet therapy). Strong SMF (8 T) aligns osteoblasts and orients new bone (Kotani 2002). Clinical SMF pain trials are mixed: positive 450 G insoles in 375 DPN patients (Weintraub 2003) and 300-500 G in post-polio (Vallbona 1997), a modest bracelet effect of uncertain specificity (Harlow 2004), and a meta-analysis of nine VAS trials showing no effect (Pittler 2007). Colbert 2008/2009 show most trials lack adequate dosimetry (61%).

discriminating_evidence.finding: SMF effects on Ca2+/Na+ channels via phospholipid anisotropy with thermotropic phase-transition dependence.

targets.name: Lorentz force, Hall and magnetohydrodynamic effects (blood flow, vestibular)
targets.driver_explanation: Lorentz/MHD effects scale with B x velocity (induced field v x B) or J x B body force, not with dB/dt, and become significant only at tesla levels: Roberts 2011 found nystagmus proportional to static field in 3 T and 7 T scanners (little or none near 0.7 T) explained by Lorentz force on endolymph; Tenforde 2005 reports no hemodynamic effects at 1.5 T and SA-node current density above 100 mA/m2 only above 5 T; aortic flow reduction 1.3% (5 T), 4.9% (10 T), 10.4% (15 T); Kinouchi 1996 finds MHD flow reduction only above about 10 T. ICNIRP 2009 sets 2 T (head/trunk occupational), 8 T (limbs) and 400 mT (public). At PEMF mT levels my computed values are tiny: v x B with v = 0.5 m/s and B = 2 mT gives 1 mV/m, and a J x B body force with J = 0.5 A/m2 (E = 1 V/m, sigma = 0.5 S/m) at 2 mT is about 1e-3 N/m3, i.e. 1e-7 of gravity body force (rho*g = 1e4 N/m3).

targets.window_summary: Lorentz/Hall/MHD effects are negligible at PEMF peak fields of 1-50 mT (computed v x B about 1-25 mV/m, force ~1e-7 of gravity) and become measurable only at about 1-7 T (vestibular, proportional to B) and relevant to cardiovascular function above about 5 T.
targets.replication_status: multiple independent sources (clinical, animal, modelling, standards)
targets.caveats: Computed estimates rely on assumed v = 0.5 m/s, sigma = 0.5 S/m and a J = 0.5 A/m2 at E = 1 V/m; Roberts 2011 threshold extrapolation is a linear guess. ICNIRP numbers come from a fetched summary of the guideline text and should be checked against the PDF if used in a calculator.

targets.name: Decision-test record: experiments that discriminate B-driven from dB/dt/E-driven effects
targets.driver_explanation: Discriminating designs in the library: (1) constant B with variable induced E using multi-ring Faraday geometry (Liburdy 1992: E at constant B governed Ca2+ influx; a pure E field gave the same effect), versus the same trick applied to MCF-7 growth (Harland & Liburdy 1997: B, not E, associated). (2) Static vs ELF equivalence (Fedele 2014: 0, 3, 50 Hz same effect, so B). (3) Constant B x f at different B and f (Prato 2011: constant effect, so dB/dt-like). (4) Selective removal of components (Choleris 2002: static nulling did not reproduce shielding; E screening did not either). (5) Orientation/angle tests at fixed amplitude (Prato 1996; Blackman 1990; Ritz 2004). (6) Dose-response saturation (Ishido 2001: 1.2 vs 100 uT same). Different endpoints therefore give different answers: the same lab line produced an E metric in one system and a B metric in another, so no single driver applies across targets.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Multi-ring annular plate: induced E varied at constant 22 mT, 60 Hz, vs pure E exposure
discriminating_evidence.finding: Ca2+ influx tracked induced E (1.7 mV/cm = 0.17 V/m reported) and a pure E field of equal strength matched it (erratum exists).

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Faraday-law design for B vs induced E
discriminating_evidence.finding: Melatonin/tamoxifen block tracked B, not induced E.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Static vs 3 Hz vs 50 Hz at 300 uT
discriminating_evidence.finding: Same effect: B-driven (dB/dt from 0 to 0.094 T/s computed).

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Constant B x f at 4 frequencies
discriminating_evidence.finding: Constant attenuation: dB/dt-like.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Static nulling vs mu-metal vs E screening
discriminating_evidence.finding: Only shielding worked: time-varying B component.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Angle between AC and DC at fixed AC
discriminating_evidence.finding: Effect varies with angle, not with constant induced current.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: 1.2 vs 100 uT
discriminating_evidence.finding: Same effect at 83-fold different B and dB/dt: saturation.

thresholds.endpoint: Increase in Ca2+ influx in mitogen-activated thymocytes (induced E metric)
thresholds.B_note: Reported 22 mT, 60 Hz; rms/peak not stated; treated as nominal peak.
thresholds.E_geometry: Reported induced E 1.7 mV/cm (= 0.17 V/m) in the annular culture plate (dish scale)
thresholds.note: Erratum exists (PMID 10930587). Computed back-radius r = 2E/(dB/dt) = 0.041 m (plate-scale consistency check, my computation).

targets.window_summary: No universal driver: Ca2+ influx in lymphocytes followed induced E (0.17 V/m at 22 mT, 60 Hz; computed dB/dt 8.3 T/s), fly circadian and MCF-7 data follow B, mouse shielding analgesia follows B x f (dB/dt-like).
targets.replication_status: mixed - several individual decision tests, mostly single-lab
targets.caveats: Liburdy-lab studies (1992, 1993, 1997) share an author with a published erratum on the 1992 paper. Not every claimed mechanism has had a B-vs-E test.

targets.name: Physical plausibility (kT, ELF theory) and exposure-standard context for B-driven mechanisms
targets.driver_explanation: Valberg 1997 concludes residential-level ELF effects (<=2 uT) are implausible and that effects above 10 uT would be plausible only through temporal averaging plus a magnetic-moment transducer; resonance mechanisms conflict with accepted physics. Binhi & Rubin 2007 counter that the 'kT paradox' rests on assumptions that may not hold for magnetic nanoparticles, long-lived rotational states or radical-pair spins. Brocklehurst & McLauchlan 1996 and Kattnig 2016 bound radical-pair mechanisms by lifetimes and relaxation. The ICNIRP 2010 guideline (existing ref icnirp2010) treats induced E as the basic restriction (CNS 10-25 Hz: 0.05 V/m occupational, 0.01 V/m public rms) with reference B of 1 mT occupational and 0.2 mT general public (50/60 Hz, rms), i.e. standards operate on E, not on B. WHO EHC 238 (2007) and the SCENIHR 2015 opinion (not in PubMed; read via fetched summaries) state that no accepted biophysical mechanism explains low-level ELF health effects; WHO states established acute effects occur at well above 100 uT through induced E and currents.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Physics review of mechanisms
discriminating_evidence.finding: <=2 uT implausible; >10 uT only with averaging plus magnetic-moment transducer (abstract only).

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Critique of the kT argument
discriminating_evidence.finding: Specific loopholes (nanoparticles, rotational states, radical pairs, proton moments) can in principle evade kT.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Existing library ref ICNIRP 2010 (guideline numbers from fetched icnirp.org text)
discriminating_evidence.finding: Basic restrictions on internal E (CNS 0.01 V/m public at 10-25 Hz) and reference B 0.2 mT public, 1 mT occupational at 50/60 Hz.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Existing library ref (Adair 1991)
discriminating_evidence.finding: Contents not re-read in this pass.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Radical-pair theory
discriminating_evidence.finding: Lifetime and chemistry limit freely diffusing pairs.

discriminating_evidence.design_feature: Relaxation simulations
discriminating_evidence.finding: Microsecond lifetimes optimal; long coherence unlikely.

thresholds.B_note: Reference level 0.2 mT rms at 50/60 Hz; peak = rms x sqrt(2), computed.
thresholds.note: Fetched from icnirp.org guideline text. At 60 Hz the same 0.2 mT rms.

thresholds.B_note: Reference level 1 mT rms at 50/60 Hz; peak computed.

thresholds.endpoint: ICNIRP basic restriction, CNS tissue of the head, 10-25 Hz, general public
thresholds.E_geometry: Internal E, rms, CNS tissue (10-25 Hz); occupational 0.05 V/m
thresholds.note: All tissues 1 Hz-3 kHz: 0.4 V/m public, 0.8 V/m occupational; magnetophosphene threshold ~5 mT at 20 Hz (retinal E ~50-100 mV/m); PNS ~4-6 V/m.

thresholds.endpoint: Plausibility floor for ELF magnetic effects (physics review)
thresholds.B_note: Effects at <=2 uT judged implausible; >10 uT (0.01 mT) possibly plausible via averaging + moment transducer (not a measured threshold).
thresholds.note: Used only as a benchmark for credibility, not a dose-response.

targets.window_summary: Credibility benchmark: physics reviews put the plausibility boundary between about 2 and 10 uT; ICNIRP 2010 reference B is 0.2 mT (public) / 1 mT (occupational) rms at 50/60 Hz, derived from induced-E basic restrictions (0.01-0.05 V/m CNS at 10-25 Hz).
targets.replication_status: consensus bodies (WHO, SCENIHR) vs individual positive studies
targets.caveats: WHO EHC 238 and SCENIHR 2015 are not PubMed-indexed and were read through fetched summaries only; not added as refs. ICNIRP numbers came from a fetched summary of the PDF.

new_refs.authors_short: Usselman RJ, Hill I, Singel DJ, Martino CF
new_refs.title: Spin biochemistry modulates reactive oxygen species (ROS) production by radio frequency magnetic fields
new_refs.summary: Rat pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells in a 45 uT static field plus 7 MHz RF at 10 uT rms showed lower superoxide and higher H2O2; authors attribute this to flavin-semiquinone / superoxide radical-pair singlet-triplet modulation.

new_refs.authors_short: Castello PR, Hill I, Sivo F, et al.
new_refs.title: Inhibition of cellular proliferation and enhancement of hydrogen peroxide production in fibrosarcoma cell line by weak radio frequency magnetic fields
new_refs.summary: HT1080 cells in a 45 uT vertical static field plus a perpendicular 5 or 10 MHz RF field of 10 uT rms: cell number fell by up to 30% (10 MHz, day 2) and H2O2 rose 55% after 8 h of 10 MHz exposure.

new_refs.authors_short: Usselman RJ, Chavarriaga C, Castello PR, et al.
new_refs.title: The Quantum Biology of Reactive Oxygen Species Partitioning Impacts Cellular Bioenergetics
new_refs.summary: In HUVEC, oscillating fields at the Zeeman-resonance condition shifted the superoxide/H2O2 product ratio, and the response depended on field orientation and altered respiration and glycolysis rates.

new_refs.authors_short: Austvold CK, Keable SM, Procopio M, Usselman RJ
new_refs.title: Quantitative measurements of reactive oxygen species partitioning in electron transfer flavoenzyme magnetic field sensing
new_refs.summary: Recombinant human electron-transfer flavoprotein reoxidation, compared between 20 nT and 50 uT static fields, gave about 13% less H2O2 (singlet product) and 10% more superoxide (triplet product) relative to 50 uT, matching radical-pair yield calculations.

new_refs.authors_short: Sherrard RM, Morellini N, Jourdan N, et al.
new_refs.title: Low-intensity electromagnetic fields induce human cryptochrome to modulate intracellular reactive oxygen species
new_refs.summary: A 10 Hz pulsed field with about 2 mT peak (non-therapeutic device) raised ROS within 15 min in cryptochrome-expressing cells, slowed growth and altered gene expression; Drosophila larvae avoided the field only under blue light, and cryptochrome knock-out or mu-metal shielding abolished the effects.

new_refs.authors_short: Landler L, Keays DA
new_refs.title: Cryptochrome: The magnetosensor with a sinister side?
new_refs.summary: Commentary accompanying Sherrard et al. that frames the cryptochrome-ROS result as potentially linking animal magnetoreception, PEMF therapy and power-line epidemiology, while stressing the field's history of skepticism.

new_refs.authors_short: Lohof AM, Dufor T, Sherrard RM
new_refs.title: Neural Circuit Repair by Low-Intensity rTMS
new_refs.summary: Review stating that low-intensity rTMS-driven cerebellar climbing-fibre repair depends on the stimulation pattern and on cryptochrome, and proposing action through cryptochrome signalling rather than induced currents (abstract only seen).

new_refs.authors_short: Ikeya N, Woodward JR
new_refs.title: Cellular autofluorescence is magnetic field sensitive
new_refs.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
new_refs.summary: Single-cell imaging of HeLa autofluorescence shows a magnetic-field effect up to 25 mT with half-saturation near 18.0 mT and a saturating amplitude of 3.7%, consistent with a triplet-born flavin radical pair.

new_refs.authors_short: Antill LM, Woodward JR
new_refs.title: Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide Photochemistry Is Magnetic Field Sensitive at Physiological pH
new_refs.summary: Time-resolved FAD photochemistry in water shows a magnetic field effect even at pH 8, where it is about 75% smaller than at pH 2.3.

new_refs.authors_short: Fedele G, Edwards MD, Bhutani S, et al.
new_refs.title: Genetic analysis of circadian responses to low frequency electromagnetic fields in Drosophila melanogaster
new_refs.summary: In a shielded apparatus, Drosophila circadian period and activity responded to 3-50 Hz fields in a cryptochrome- and blue-light-dependent way; a 300 uT static field, 3 Hz and 50 Hz fields produced the same period effect, but mouse SCN slices showed no effect.

new_refs.authors_short: Giachello CNG, Scrutton NS, Jones AR, Baines RA
new_refs.title: Magnetic Fields Modulate Blue-Light-Dependent Regulation of Neuronal Firing by Cryptochrome
new_refs.summary: A 100 mT field potentiated blue-light-driven depolarisation, input resistance rise and firing in Drosophila larval motoneurons ectopically expressing cryptochrome.

new_refs.authors_short: Ahmad M, Galland P, Ritz T, Wiltschko R, Wiltschko W
new_refs.title: Magnetic intensity affects cryptochrome-dependent responses in Arabidopsis thaliana
new_refs.summary: Raising the static field from 33-44 uT to 500 uT enhanced blue-light hypocotyl inhibition, anthocyanin accumulation and CRY2 degradation in Arabidopsis, not under red light or in cryptochrome mutants.

new_refs.authors_short: Pooam M, Arthaut LD, Burdick D, et al.
new_refs.title: Magnetic sensitivity mediated by the Arabidopsis blue-light receptor cryptochrome occurs during flavin reoxidation in the dark
new_refs.summary: A 500 uT static field enhanced cryptochrome-1 responses even when applied only during the dark intervals between light pulses, placing the magnetically sensitive step in flavin reoxidation.

new_refs.authors_short: Hammad M, Albaqami M, Pooam M, et al.
new_refs.title: Cryptochrome mediated magnetic sensitivity in Arabidopsis occurs independently of light-induced electron transfer to the flavin
new_refs.summary: With 5 min light / 10 min dark cycles, a 500 uT field worked when given only in the dark intervals but not when given only during the light, ruling out forward electron transfer as the magnetosensitive step.

new_refs.authors_short: Ritz T, Thalau P, Phillips JB, Wiltschko R, Wiltschko W
new_refs.title: Resonance effects indicate a radical-pair mechanism for avian magnetic compass
new_refs.summary: Migratory robins were disoriented by 0.1-10 MHz broadband or 7 MHz fields, and the 7 MHz effect depended on the angle to the geomagnetic field (normal orientation when parallel, disorientation at 24 and 48 degrees).

new_refs.authors_short: Rodgers CT, Hore PJ
new_refs.title: Chemical magnetoreception in birds: the radical pair mechanism
new_refs.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
new_refs.summary: Physical-chemistry review of the chemical requirements for a radical-pair compass sensitive to an Earth-strength (about 50 uT) field and of cryptochrome as a candidate.

new_refs.authors_short: Maeda K, Henbest KB, Cintolesi F, et al.
new_refs.title: Chemical compass model of avian magnetoreception
new_refs.summary: A carotenoid-porphyrin-fullerene model system showed radical-pair lifetime changes at 50 uT or less and an anisotropic response, demonstrating that chemistry can in principle sense geomagnetic-strength fields.

new_refs.authors_short: Brocklehurst B, McLauchlan KA
new_refs.title: Free radical mechanism for the effects of environmental electromagnetic fields on biological systems
new_refs.summary: Theory paper stressing that low-field radical-pair effects depend on radical lifetime and chemistry, and arguing that freely diffusing radical pairs are unlikely to give significant biological effects.

new_refs.authors_short: Kattnig DR, Solov'yov IA, Hore PJ
new_refs.title: Electron spin relaxation in cryptochrome-based magnetoreception
new_refs.summary: Simulations for Arabidopsis cryptochrome-1 imply optimal radical-pair lifetimes of microseconds and spin relaxation too fast to explain the long coherence invoked for RF disruption of the avian compass.

new_refs.authors_short: Zadeh-Haghighi H, Simon C
new_refs.title: Magnetic field effects in biology from the perspective of the radical pair mechanism
new_refs.summary: Review of weak static, hypomagnetic and oscillating field effects in biology and of how far a radical-pair mechanism can explain them.

new_refs.authors_short: Van Huizen AV, Morton JM, Kinsey LJ, et al.
new_refs.title: Weak magnetic fields alter stem cell-mediated growth
new_refs.summary: Static weak fields below 1 mT raised or lowered planarian regeneration depending on field strength, via ROS accumulation and Hsp70 expression.

new_refs.authors_short: Binhi VN, Prato FS
new_refs.title: Biological effects of the hypomagnetic field: An analytical review of experiments and theories
new_refs.summary: Extensive review concluding that hypomagnetic-field effects show no statistical correlation with field magnitude, inhomogeneity, exposure type or duration, arguing against a single common target.

new_refs.authors_short: Carter CS, Huang SC, Searby CC, et al.
new_refs.title: Exposure to Static Magnetic and Electric Fields Treats Type 2 Diabetes
new_refs.summary: Combined static magnetic (about 3 mT) and static electric (about 7 kV/m) fields lowered mitochondrial superoxide, shifted systemic redox and improved glucose tolerance in diabetic mice; in hepatoma cells 3.0 mT was effective and 0.5 mT was not; SOD2 abolished the effect.

new_refs.authors_short: Binhi VN, Rubin AB
new_refs.title: Magnetobiology: the kT paradox and possible solutions
new_refs.summary: Argues the kT objection rests on assumptions that may not hold for magnetic nanoparticles, long-lived rotational states, radical-pair spins or proton moments in water.

new_refs.authors_short: Valberg PA, Kavet R, Rafferty CN
new_refs.title: Can low-level 50/60 Hz electric and magnetic fields cause biological effects?
new_refs.summary: Physics review concluding that effects of residential ELF fields at or below 2 uT are implausible and that effects above 10 uT would at most be plausible via temporal averaging plus a magnetic-moment transducer; resonance mechanisms conflict with accepted physics (abstract only).

new_refs.authors_short: Lednev VV
new_refs.title: Possible mechanism for the influence of weak magnetic fields on biological systems
new_refs.summary: Proposes that a Ca2+ ion bound in a protein acts as a charged oscillator whose transition probability changes under combined static and alternating fields, peaking when the AC frequency equals the ion cyclotron frequency or a harmonic.

new_refs.authors_short: Blanchard JP, Blackman CF
new_refs.title: Clarification and application of an ion parametric resonance model for magnetic field interactions with biological systems
new_refs.summary: Corrects and extends Lednev's model into an IPR model whose predicted response forms depend on Bac, Bdc, AC frequency and ion charge-to-mass ratio, and proposes direct tests.

new_refs.authors_short: Blackman CF, Blanchard JP, Benane SG, House DE
new_refs.title: Empirical test of an ion parametric resonance model for magnetic field interactions with PC-12 cells
new_refs.summary: NGF-stimulated neurite outgrowth in PC-12 cells was tested with 45 Hz Bac of 77-468 mG rms at 366 mG Bdc, an off-resonance condition, and 25 Hz at 203 mG Bdc; all responses matched IPR predictions.

new_refs.authors_short: Engström S
new_refs.title: Dynamic properties of Lednev's parametric resonance mechanism
new_refs.summary: Dynamic model of the Lednev oscillator with thermal noise confirming its main results, requiring the excited-state lifetime to exceed the field period, and proposing a test depending only on the B1/B0 ratio.

new_refs.authors_short: Machlup S
new_refs.title: Ion parametric resonance: resolving the signal-to-noise-ratio paradox
new_refs.summary: Argues the IPR signal-to-noise paradox raised by Adair is resolved by coherent absorption of many ELF quanta that free a single trapped ion.

new_refs.authors_short: Adair RK
new_refs.title: Criticism of Lednev's mechanism for the influence of weak magnetic fields on biological systems
new_refs.summary: Physics critique giving four independent reasons why a Lednev-type cyclotron-frequency mechanism cannot operate in the geomagnetic field.

new_refs.authors_short: Sandweiss J
new_refs.title: On the cyclotron resonance model of ion transport
new_refs.summary: Shows ions at the Earth-field cyclotron frequency would have gyration radii near 50 m and collision damping times below 1e-10 s versus the roughly 1e-2 s needed, so the cyclotron model violates basic physics.

new_refs.authors_short: Halle B
new_refs.title: On the cyclotron resonance mechanism for magnetic field effects on transmembrane ion conductivity
new_refs.summary: Argues that the original cyclotron-resonance model breaks classical mechanics and that dynamic friction in fluid media precludes significant magnetic effects on membrane ion transport.

new_refs.authors_short: Smith SD, McLeod BR, Liboff AR, Cooksey K
new_refs.title: Calcium cyclotron resonance and diatom mobility
new_refs.summary: Diatom (Amphora) motility, a proxy for Ca2+ transport, showed a sharp resonance at the predicted Ca2+ cyclotron frequency, a dose-response to AC flux density and responses at odd harmonics.

new_refs.authors_short: Reese JA, Frazier ME, Morris JE, Buschbom RL, Miller DL
new_refs.title: Evaluation of changes in diatom mobility after exposure to 16-Hz electromagnetic fields
new_refs.summary: A 16 Hz, 20.9 uT AC field parallel to a 20.9 uT horizontal DC field increased diatom motion at 0.25 mM Ca2+, but the response was not reproducible enough to test frequency dependence.

new_refs.authors_short: Parkinson WC, Hanks CT
new_refs.title: Search for cyclotron resonance in cells in vitro
new_refs.summary: Fura-2 measurements in four cell lines (BALB/c3T3, L929, V-79, ROS) found no change in cytosolic Ca2+ under resonant or non-resonant ELF fields.

new_refs.authors_short: Coulton LA, Barker AT
new_refs.title: Magnetic fields and intracellular calcium: effects on lymphocytes exposed to conditions for 'cyclotron resonance'
new_refs.summary: Mouse lymphocytes exposed for 60 min to Ca2+ cyclotron-resonance conditions at 16 and 50 Hz (DC varied up to 25% either side) showed no change in intracellular Ca2+, while concanavalin A positive controls did.

new_refs.authors_short: Blackman CF, Benane SG, House DE, Elliott DJ
new_refs.title: Importance of alignment between local DC magnetic field and an oscillating magnetic field in responses of brain tissue in vitro and in vivo
new_refs.summary: In chick brain tissue, a 315 Hz field (61 nT rms, 15 V/m rms in air) released Ca2+ only when the AC and DC magnetic components were perpendicular, not parallel.

new_refs.authors_short: Blackman CF, Benane SG, House DE
new_refs.title: The influence of temperature during electric- and magnetic-field-induced alteration of calcium-ion release from in vitro brain tissue
new_refs.summary: At 16 Hz (14.1 V/m rms, 64 nT rms) chick brain Ca2+ efflux was enhanced, reduced or unchanged depending on sample temperature and its drift during exposure, which may explain poor inter-lab reproducibility.

new_refs.authors_short: Blackman CF, Most B
new_refs.title: A scheme for incorporating DC magnetic fields into epidemiological studies of EMF exposure
new_refs.summary: Uses chick-brain Ca2+ data to define 'active' AC/DC combinations and proposes an exposure score; for 60 Hz and 50 Hz the highest scores fall at DC fields of 506 mG and 422 mG.

new_refs.authors_short: Lindström E, Lindström P, Berglund A, Lundgren E, Mild KH
new_refs.title: Intracellular calcium oscillations in a T-cell line after exposure to extremely-low-frequency magnetic fields with variable frequencies and flux densities
new_refs.summary: Jurkat cells showed Ca2+ oscillations to sinusoidal fields at 0.15 mT across 5-100 Hz with a broad peak at 50 Hz, and a threshold dose-response at 50 Hz with no effect below 0.04 mT and a plateau at 0.15 mT.

new_refs.authors_short: Wey HE, Conover DP, Mathias P, Toraason M, Lotz WG
new_refs.title: 50-Hertz magnetic field and calcium transients in Jurkat cells: results of a research and public information dissemination (RAPID) program study
new_refs.summary: Blinded attempt to repeat Lindstrom with 1.5 G, 50 Hz in Jurkat cells found Ca2+ transient incidence of 16.5% (field), 14.6% (sham) and 14.2% (no field), not significantly different.

new_refs.authors_short: Fitzsimmons RJ, Ryaby JT, Magee FP, Baylink DJ
new_refs.title: Combined magnetic fields increased net calcium flux in bone cells
new_refs.summary: A low-amplitude combined (AC plus DC) field inducing a calculated potential gradient of 1e-5 V/m increased net Ca2+ flux in human osteoblast-like cells with a frequency peak at 15.3-16.3 Hz and bandwidth near 1 Hz (abstract only).

new_refs.authors_short: Fitzsimmons RJ, Ryaby JT, Magee FP, Baylink DJ
new_refs.title: IGF-II receptor number is increased in TE-85 osteosarcoma cells by combined magnetic fields
new_refs.summary: A 15.3 Hz combined field (calculated maximum induced potential of 1e-5 V/m in medium) given for 30 min raised IGF-II receptor number frequency-dependently without changing IGF-I receptors.

new_refs.authors_short: Fitzsimmons RJ, Ryaby JT, Mohan S, Magee FP, Baylink DJ
new_refs.title: Combined magnetic fields increase insulin-like growth factor-II in TE-85 human osteosarcoma bone cell cultures
new_refs.summary: Only 10 min of combined-field exposure raised IGF-II release and 24 h DNA synthesis in TE-85 cells, blocked by anti-IGF-II antibody and stronger at low cell density.

new_refs.authors_short: Zhadin MN, Novikov VV, Barnes FS, Pergola NF
new_refs.title: Combined action of static and alternating magnetic fields on ionic current in aqueous glutamic acid solution
new_refs.summary: In a cell-free glutamic acid solution, parallel DC and AC fields produced a 20-30% current peak at the cyclotron frequency (1-10 Hz sweep), proportional to the static field and present only at AC amplitudes of 0.02-0.08 uT.

new_refs.authors_short: Zhadin MN, Deryugina ON, Pisachenko TM
new_refs.title: Influence of combined DC and AC magnetic fields on rat behavior
new_refs.summary: Rat open-field activity fell at the Ca2+ cyclotron frequency and rose at the Mg2+ frequency, qualitatively the same at 50 uT and 500 uT DC with proportionally scaled AC frequency and amplitude; other ions had no effect.

new_refs.authors_short: Bauréus Koch CLM, Sommarin M, Persson BRR, Salford LG, Eberhardt JL
new_refs.title: Interaction between weak low frequency magnetic fields and cell membranes
new_refs.summary: Ca-45 efflux from purified plasma-membrane vesicles (30 min, 32 C) with 27-37 uT static and 7-72 Hz, 13-114 uT peak AC fields confirmed quantitatively the Blanchard resonance model.

new_refs.authors_short: Blackman CF, Benane SG, House DE
new_refs.title: The influence of 1.2 microT, 60 Hz magnetic fields on melatonin- and tamoxifen-induced inhibition of MCF-7 cell growth
new_refs.summary: Independent replication: 1.2 uT rms, 60 Hz removed the 16.7% melatonin growth inhibition and cut tamoxifen inhibition from 18.6/25% to 8.7/13.1% (days 6/7) in MCF-7 cells, with blinded counts.

new_refs.authors_short: Liburdy RP, Sloma TR, Sokolic R, Yaswen P
new_refs.title: ELF magnetic fields, breast cancer, and melatonin: 60 Hz fields block melatonin's oncostatic action on ER+ breast cancer cell proliferation
new_refs.summary: 60 Hz fields near 12 mG (1.2 uT) blocked melatonin's 18-27% growth inhibition of MCF-7 cells whereas about 2-2.5 mG did not, suggesting a threshold between 2 and 12 mG.

new_refs.authors_short: Harland JD, Liburdy RP
new_refs.title: Environmental magnetic fields inhibit the antiproliferative action of tamoxifen and melatonin in a human breast cancer cell line
new_refs.summary: Using a Faraday's-law design to separate the 1.2 uT magnetic field from the associated induced electric field, the authors found the magnetic component was associated with the block of tamoxifen and melatonin action.

new_refs.authors_short: Ishido M, Nitta H, Kabuto M
new_refs.title: Magnetic fields (MF) of 50 Hz at 1.2 microT as well as 100 microT cause uncoupling of inhibitory pathways of adenylyl cyclase mediated by melatonin 1a receptor in MF-sensitive MCF-7 cells
new_refs.summary: In MF-sensitive MCF-7 cells, 3-7 day exposure to 100 uT blocked melatonin-induced cAMP inhibition, and 1.2 uT gave the same effect on melatonin signalling, i.e. no extra effect for an 83-fold larger field.

new_refs.authors_short: Girgert R, Schimming H, Korner W, Grundker C, Hanf V
new_refs.title: Induction of tamoxifen resistance in breast cancer cells by ELF electromagnetic fields
new_refs.summary: 50 Hz exposure shifted tamoxifen dose-response curves of two MCF-7 clones to higher concentrations, with a maximal shift at 1.2 uT.

new_refs.authors_short: Girgert R, Hanf V, Emons G, Grundker C
new_refs.title: Signal transduction of the melatonin receptor MT1 is disrupted in breast cancer cells by electromagnetic fields
new_refs.summary: A 48 h exposure to 1.2 uT, 50 Hz abolished melatonin-induced CREB binding to the BRCA-1 promoter and altered melatonin-regulated gene expression in MCF-7 cells.

new_refs.authors_short: Leman ES, Sisken BF, Zimmer S, Anderson KW
new_refs.title: Studies of the interactions between melatonin and 2 Hz, 0.3 mT PEMF on the proliferation and invasion of human breast cancer cells
new_refs.summary: A 2 Hz, 0.3 mT pulsed field did not alter melatonin's growth inhibition or the invasiveness of three breast cancer lines, unlike reports for 60 Hz power-line fields.

new_refs.authors_short: Liburdy RP
new_refs.title: Calcium signaling in lymphocytes and ELF fields. Evidence for an electric field metric and a site of interaction involving the calcium ion channel
new_refs.summary: Mitogen-stimulated rat thymocytes showed larger Ca2+ influx in a 22 mT, 60 Hz field (induced E 1.7 mV/cm); a multi-ring annular plate showed dependence on induced E at constant B, and a pure E field of equal strength acted similarly (note: an erratum to this paper exists).

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS, Carson JJ, Ossenkopp KP, Kavaliers M
new_refs.title: Possible mechanisms by which extremely low frequency magnetic fields affect opioid function
new_refs.summary: In snails, loss of opioid analgesia depended nonlinearly on 60 Hz peak amplitude (0-547 uT), showed frequency windows at 141 uT, and varied with the parallel static field, which the authors read as direct field detection rather than induced current.

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS, Kavaliers M, Carson JJ
new_refs.title: Behavioural evidence that magnetic field effects in the land snail, Cepaea nemoralis, might not depend on magnetite or induced electric currents
new_refs.summary: With 78 uT static and 299 uT peak 60 Hz fields, varying the angle between them changed the analgesia reduction from about 20% (0 and 90 degrees) to about 50% (50-70 degrees); a constant induced current or a magnetite torque would not predict this.

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS, Kavaliers M, Thomas AW
new_refs.title: Extremely low frequency magnetic fields can either increase or decrease analgaesia in the land snail depending on field and light conditions
new_refs.summary: Snail fields of 141-414 uT peak set to Lednev PRM conditions for Ca2+ reduced, did not change, or increased opioid analgesia as predicted, K+ settings increased it (glibenclamide-sensitive), and all effects needed light.

new_refs.authors_short: Kavaliers M, Prato FS
new_refs.title: Light-dependent effects of magnetic fields on nitric oxide activation in the land snail
new_refs.summary: Brief 60 Hz exposure potentiated, in a light-dependent way, the inhibitory effect of L-arginine on opioid analgesia in snails, implicating nitric oxide in light-dependent magnetic effects.

new_refs.authors_short: Kavaliers M, Choleris E, Prato FS, Ossenkopp K
new_refs.title: Evidence for the involvement of nitric oxide and nitric oxide synthase in the modulation of opioid-induced antinociception and the inhibitory effects of exposure to 60-Hz magnetic fields in the land snail
new_refs.summary: In snails, 15 min of 60 Hz, 141 uT peak reduced enkephalinase-induced antinociception; L-NAME reduced and an NO donor increased this magnetic inhibition.

new_refs.authors_short: Thomas AW, Kavaliers M, Prato FS, Ossenkopp KP
new_refs.title: Antinociceptive effects of a pulsed magnetic field in the land snail, Cepaea nemoralis
new_refs.summary: A 15 min exposure to a specific frequency-modulated pulsed field of about 100 uT peak (Cnp) induced analgesia in snails, partly naloxone-sensitive, while two other pulsed waveforms were ineffective.

new_refs.authors_short: Thomas AW, Kavaliers M, Prato FS, Ossenkopp KP
new_refs.title: Pulsed magnetic field induced 'analgesia' in the land snail, Cepaea nemoralis, and the effects of mu, delta, and kappa opioid receptor agonists/antagonists
new_refs.summary: Cnp-induced snail analgesia was reduced by naloxone, mu and delta antagonists but not a kappa antagonist, indicating partial delta (and some mu) opioid receptor mediation.

new_refs.authors_short: Kavaliers M, Ossenkopp KP
new_refs.title: Magnetic fields inhibit opioid-mediated 'analgesic' behaviours of the terrestrial snail, Cepaea nemoralis
new_refs.summary: A 0.5 Hz rotating field of 1.5-8.0 G (15-30 min) reduced opioid and stress-induced analgesia in snails, and Ca2+-channel antagonists/agonist modulated the effect.

new_refs.authors_short: Kavaliers M, Ossenkopp KP
new_refs.title: Calcium channel involvement in magnetic field inhibition of morphine-induced analgesia
new_refs.summary: In mice, 60 min of a 0.5 Hz rotating field reduced morphine analgesia, with dihydropyridine and other Ca2+-channel drugs modulating the inhibition.

new_refs.authors_short: Shupak NM, Hensel JM, Cross-Mellor SK, et al.
new_refs.title: Analgesic and behavioral effects of a 100 microT specific pulsed extremely low frequency magnetic field on control and morphine treated CF-1 mice
new_refs.summary: A 100 uT specific pulsed field prolonged hot-plate latency in mice by an amount equivalent to about 5 mg/kg morphine and offset morphine-induced hyperactivity.

new_refs.authors_short: Shupak NM, Prato FS, Thomas AW
new_refs.title: Human exposure to a specific pulsed magnetic field: effects on thermal sensory and pain thresholds
new_refs.summary: In two double-blind studies (n=39, n=31), 30 min of a specific pulsed field raised experimental heat-pain thresholds but not sensory thresholds, with a gender interaction and possible placebo contribution.

new_refs.authors_short: Shupak NM, McKay JC, Nielson WR, Rollman GB, Prato FS, Thomas AW
new_refs.title: Exposure to a specific pulsed low-frequency magnetic field: a double-blind placebo-controlled study of effects on pain ratings in rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia patients
new_refs.summary: A single 30 min exposure (up to 400 uT peak, below 3 kHz) reduced McGill pain ratings versus sham in 13 rheumatoid arthritis and 18 fibromyalgia patients; small acute double-blind trial.

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS
new_refs.title: Non-thermal extremely low frequency magnetic field effects on opioid related behaviors: Snails to humans, mechanisms to therapy
new_refs.summary: Author's own account of 30 years of ELF-MF effects on nociception from snails to humans, explicitly not a balanced review, linking the work to animal orientation research.

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS, Desjardins-Holmes D, Keenliside LD, DeMoor JM, Robertson JA, Stodilka RZ, Thomas AW
new_refs.title: The detection threshold for extremely low frequency magnetic fields may be below 1000 nT-Hz in mice
new_refs.summary: Mu-metal-shielding analgesia in mice was attenuated by reintroduced 30 and 120 Hz fields of 25-500 nT peak in proportion to amplitude, and at a constant 6000 nT-Hz product (12.5-100 Hz) attenuation was constant, giving a detection threshold at or below 1000 nT-Hz.

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS, Desjardins-Holmes D, Keenliside LD, McKay JC, Robertson JA, Thomas AW
new_refs.title: Light alters nociceptive effects of magnetic field shielding in mice: intensity and wavelength considerations
new_refs.summary: Shielding analgesia in mice was abolished by blue (465 nm) or UV light but not red light, with a blue-light threshold near 5e16 photons/s/m2, paralleling photoreceptor-based magnetoreception.

new_refs.authors_short: Prato FS, Robertson JA, Desjardins D, Hensel J, Thomas AW
new_refs.title: Daily repeated magnetic field shielding induces analgesia in CD-1 mice
new_refs.summary: One hour per day in a mu-metal box for 10 days produced analgesia peaking on days 4-6, comparable to 5 mg/kg morphine and abolished by naloxone.

new_refs.authors_short: Choleris E, Del Seppia C, Thomas AW, et al.
new_refs.title: Shielding, but not zeroing of the ambient magnetic field reduces stress-induced analgesia in mice
new_refs.summary: Independently replicated in Pisa and London: mu-metal shielding reduced stress-induced analgesia, whereas nulling the static component with Helmholtz coils or shielding the electric field with copper did not, implicating the extremely weak time-varying component.

new_refs.authors_short: Ubeda A, Leal J, Trillo MA, Jimenez MA, Delgado JM
new_refs.title: Pulse shape of magnetic fields influences chick embryogenesis
new_refs.summary: Chick embryos exposed for 48 h to 100 Hz pulses of 0.4-104 uT had abnormalities only at 1.0 and 13.9 uT with 100 us rise times (a window), and shorter rise times (2 and 42 us) gave larger effects, strongest at 1.0 uT with 42 us.

new_refs.authors_short: Berman E, Chacon L, House D, et al.
new_refs.title: Development of chicken embryos in a pulsed magnetic field
new_refs.summary: Six-laboratory study (500 us pulses, 100 pps, 1 uT peak, 2 us edges, 48 h): pooled anomaly rate about 25% vs 19% (significant), but only two laboratories were individually significant and inter-lab variation was unexplained.

new_refs.authors_short: Davila AF, Winklhofer M, Shcherbakov VP, Petersen N
new_refs.title: Magnetic pulse affects a putative magnetoreceptor mechanism
new_refs.summary: Physical model of superparamagnetic magnetite clusters predicting chain self-assembly into a compass needle, disruption by strong oblique pulses and reassembly over hours to days, matching bird pulse-treatment results.

new_refs.authors_short: Wiltschko W, Munro U, Ford H, Wiltschko R
new_refs.title: Avian orientation: the pulse effect is mediated by the magnetite receptors in the upper beak
new_refs.summary: A strong magnetic pulse shifted silvereye headings by about 90 degrees, and local anaesthesia of the upper beak skin prevented the shift, implicating superparamagnetic magnetite structures there.

new_refs.authors_short: Gilder SA, Wack M, Kaub L, et al.
new_refs.title: Distribution of magnetic remanence carriers in the human brain
new_refs.summary: Remanence measurements on 822 specimens from seven brains show magnetite concentrated in cerebellum and brain stem (about 2x the cerebral cortex).

new_refs.authors_short: Qin S, Yin H, Yang C, et al.
new_refs.title: A magnetic protein biocompass
new_refs.summary: Reports a Drosophila iron-sulfur protein (MagR) forming a rod-like complex with cryptochrome that aligns with magnetic fields including the Earth's; physical plausibility was challenged by Meister (2016).

new_refs.authors_short: Meister M
new_refs.title: Physical limits to magnetogenetics
new_refs.summary: Quantitative analysis finding ferritin/MagR magnetic-actuation claims fall short by 5-10 orders of magnitude; ferritin torque stays far below kT at 50 mT and even forces at 5 T are ~4 log units too small, whereas permanent-moment magnetosome-sized particles could work.

new_refs.authors_short: Barbic M
new_refs.title: Possible magneto-mechanical and magneto-thermal mechanisms of ion channel activation in magnetogenetics
new_refs.summary: Considers a wider range of ferritin iron spin configurations and proposes several magneto-mechanical and magneto-thermal routes by which magnetogenetic channel activation might be physically possible.

new_refs.authors_short: Rosen AD
new_refs.title: Mechanism of action of moderate-intensity static magnetic fields on biological systems
new_refs.summary: Proposes that moderate static fields act by reorienting diamagnetically anisotropic membrane phospholipids, deforming embedded channels (Ca2+ more than Na+) and altering activation kinetics, supported by patch-clamp work.

new_refs.authors_short: Zablotskii V, Polyakova T, Lunov O, Dejneka A
new_refs.title: How a High-Gradient Magnetic Field Could Affect Cell Life
new_refs.summary: Theory that about 1 T with gradients up to 1 GT/m could change the cell membrane potential and channel gating probability via magnetic pressure and magneto-mechanical stress.

new_refs.authors_short: Kotani H, Kawaguchi H, Shimoaka T, et al.
new_refs.title: Strong static magnetic field stimulates bone formation to a definite orientation in vitro and in vivo
new_refs.summary: An 8 T static field for 60 h aligned MC3T3-E1 osteoblasts parallel to the field, increased ALP and mineralisation without changing proliferation, and oriented BMP-induced ectopic bone parallel to the field in mice.

new_refs.authors_short: Weintraub MI, Wolfe GI, Barohn RA, et al.
new_refs.title: Static magnetic field therapy for symptomatic diabetic neuropathy: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
new_refs.summary: In 375 patients wearing 450 G multipolar insoles for 4 months, burning fell 12% vs 3% (sham) and numbness/tingling 10% vs +1% in months 3-4; larger gains in those with severe baseline pain.

new_refs.authors_short: Vallbona C, Hazlewood CF, Jurida G
new_refs.title: Response of pain to static magnetic fields in postpolio patients: a double-blind pilot study
new_refs.summary: In 50 postpolio patients, 45 min with a 300-500 G device over a trigger point cut pain by 4.4 points vs 1.1 for placebo (76% vs 19% exceeded placebo effect).

new_refs.authors_short: Harlow T, Greaves C, White A, Brown L, Hart A, Ernst E
new_refs.title: Randomised controlled trial of magnetic bracelets for relieving pain in osteoarthritis of the hip and knee
new_refs.summary: In 194 patients wearing standard, weak or dummy bracelets for 12 weeks, WOMAC A pain fell 1.3 points more with standard magnets than dummy (95% CI 0.05 to 2.55), with uncertain specificity versus placebo.

new_refs.authors_short: Pittler MH, Brown EM, Ernst E
new_refs.title: Static magnets for reducing pain: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials
new_refs.summary: Meta-analysis of nine placebo-controlled VAS trials found no significant pain reduction from static magnets (weighted mean difference 2.1 mm, 95% CI -1.8 to 5.9).

new_refs.authors_short: Colbert AP, Wahbeh H, Harling N, et al.
new_refs.title: Static magnetic field therapy: a critical review of treatment parameters
new_refs.summary: Review of 56 human SMF studies finding that 34 (61%) reported too little dosimetry to allow replication and proposing a minimum reporting set.

new_refs.authors_short: Colbert AP, Markov MS, Souder JS
new_refs.title: Static magnetic field therapy: dosimetry considerations
new_refs.summary: Argues negative SMF trials are uninterpretable when field at the target tissue is not characterised and lists ten essential dosimetry parameters.

new_refs.authors_short: ICNIRP
new_refs.title: Guidelines on limits of exposure to static magnetic fields
new_refs.summary: ICNIRP static-field guidance (no abstract in PubMed); numbers used here come from the ICNIRP document text retrieved from icnirp.org.

new_refs.authors_short: Kinouchi Y, Yamaguchi H, Tenforde TS
new_refs.title: Theoretical analysis of magnetic field interactions with aortic blood flow
new_refs.summary: Finite-element Navier-Stokes analysis of aortic flow in a static field gives induced voltages and current densities, with magnetohydrodynamic flow reduction only above about 10 T.

new_refs.authors_short: Tenforde TS
new_refs.title: Magnetically induced electric fields and currents in the circulatory system
new_refs.summary: Animals at up to 1.5 T showed no hemodynamic change; models predict SA-node current density above 100 mA/m2 above 5 T and aortic flow reductions of 1.3%, 4.9% and 10.4% at 5, 10 and 15 T.

new_refs.authors_short: Roberts DC, Marcelli V, Gillen JS, Carey JP, Della Santina CC, Zee DS
new_refs.title: MRI magnetic field stimulates rotational sensors of the brain
new_refs.summary: Healthy subjects in 3 T and 7 T scanners developed nystagmus proportional to static field and independent of motion-induced voltage, polarity- and orientation-dependent, absent in labyrinthine-deficient patients, explained by a Lorentz force on endolymph.

cross_cutting_notes: 1) Decision tests. Designs that discriminate B from dB/dt/E and were run: Liburdy 1992 (Faraday multi-ring plate: Ca2+ influx followed induced E, 1.7 mV/cm = 0.17 V/m at 22 mT 60 Hz; erratum exists); Harland & Liburdy 1997 (MCF-7: B, not E); Fedele 2014 (static = 3 Hz = 50 Hz at 300 uT: B); Prato 2011 (constant B x f: dB/dt-like); Choleris 2002 (static nulling and E screening do not reproduce shielding); Prato 1996 and Blackman 1990 (angle/orientation dependence at fixed amplitude); Ishido 2001 (1.2 uT = 100 uT: saturation, so not dB/dt-scaling). Sherrard 2018's mu-metal and antiparallel-coil controls do NOT discriminate B from E because both remove B and induced E together. 2) Larmor frequency: the brief's '~1.4 MHz/mT' is a unit slip; free-electron Larmor is 28.0 MHz/mT, about 1.26 MHz at 45 uT and 1.4 MHz at 50 uT; 7 MHz RF (Usselman, Ritz) is about 5x the Larmor frequency of the ~45 uT static field. 3) Therapeutic relevance: B-driven mechanisms in this scope operate at much lower B (0.02 uT to 0.5 mT) than typical PEMF peaks (1-50 mT) or need static B0 plus orientation; the radical-pair mT-scale effects (B1/2 = 18 mT) are the one place where PEMF peak fields overlap, but they need light-activated flavin and have not been tested with pulses. 4) Credibility context (not added as refs because not in PubMed; read via fetched summaries): WHO EHC 238 (2007) restates IARC 2B for >0.3-0.4 uT childhood leukaemia and says no accepted mechanism and established acute effects only well above 100 uT via induced E and currents; SCENIHR 2015 (final opinion page) says no mechanisms identified and no experimental support for the leukaemia association. ICNIRP 2010 (existing ref icnirp2010) numbers were taken from a fetched summary of the guideline text. 5) Gaps: Fitzsimmons CMF B_ac/B_dc not retrieved (abstracts only); Hore 2012 comment, Lednev 1995 comment, Liboff 2002 comment and a Russian-language Deriugina 1996 precursor were seen but not added (no abstracts or duplicates of added refs); Dobson 2008 and Kirschvink 1996 (microwave magnetite) were judged out of scope; existing refs hore2016, barnes2015, wang2017, kirschvink1992, adair1991, liboff2009, liboff2010, pall2013, pall2022, weaver1990, gabriel1996, thomas2007 were cited but not re-read in this pass. 6) weintraub2009 (existing, PMID 19577022) is the PEMF diabetic-neuropathy study; the SMF insole RCT added here is Weintraub 2003 (PMID 12736891). 7) Liburdy-lab caution: the 1992 FEBS paper (PMID 1333413) carries an erratum (PMID 10930587, FEBS Lett 478(3):304, 2000), content not seen; the 1993 and 1997 MCF-7 papers share the senior author but were independently supported by Blackman 2001, Ishido 2001 and Girgert 2005/2010.
